Okay, take us through it properly.
A bubble sort makes repeated passes through the list comparing adjacent pairs and swapping those in the wrong order. After each pass the largest unsorted item reaches its final position at the end.
Makes sense. Keep going.
The sort stops when a pass completes with no swaps (or after n − 1 passes). It is easy to write but slow for large lists.
Right. What else do we need to know?
An insertion sort builds a sorted sub-list at the start. Each new item is taken from the unsorted part and inserted into the correct position in the sorted part, with larger items shifted along.
Got it. Keep going.
It is generally more efficient than a bubble sort, especially when the data is already nearly in order.

Bubble sort?
Compares adjacent items and swaps them if out of order, repeating passes until no swaps occur.
Insertion sort?
Builds a sorted list by inserting each item into its correct position.
